title: Rectification of Errors
outcomes: Name the stages at which errors arise and classify errors as omission, commission, principle or compensating.
Tell one-sided errors from two-sided errors and predict which ones disturb the trial balance.
Rectify errors found before the trial balance, after the trial balance (through a suspense account) and in the next accounting period (through a Profit & Loss Adjustment account).
Work out the effect of each error and its rectification on net profit.

meta.exam_tip: Rectification with a suspense account is a regular 5–10 mark question. Write the correct entry, the wrong entry, then the rectifying entry in your head for every item.

concepts.title: Where errors creep in
body: Errors can happen while recording in the journal or subsidiary books, while posting to the ledger, while totalling (casting) or carrying forward a total, while balancing an account, or while copying balances into the trial balance.
Over-casting means adding up a column to more than its true total; under-casting means less.
concepts.analogy: Like a relay race: the baton (the amount) can be dropped at any hand-over — book, ledger, total, trial balance.
concepts.work: When a difference appears, accountants retrace these stages in order: re-add the books, check postings, re-balance accounts and re-copy the trial balance.

concepts.title: Four kinds of errors
body: Errors of omission — a transaction is left out completely (both sides) or partly (only one side posted).
Errors of commission — wrong amount, wrong account of the same class (posting to Sumit instead of Amit), wrong side, wrong total, wrong balance.
Errors of principle — the accounting rule is broken: capital expenditure treated as revenue (machinery debited to Purchases) or the reverse (repairs debited to Building).
Compensating errors — two or more errors that cancel each other's effect on the trial balance.
concepts.analogy: Omission = forgot to write it; commission = wrote it wrongly; principle = did not know the rule; compensating = two wrongs that hide each other.
concepts.work: Errors of principle matter most to auditors because they misstate both profit and assets — the trial balance never catches them.

concepts.title: One-sided and two-sided errors
body: A one-sided error affects only one account (a wrong total, a posting on one side only, a wrong amount posted to one account). It disturbs the trial balance.
A two-sided error affects two accounts equally (both sides wrong in the same way). It does not disturb the trial balance and is corrected by a journal entry between the two accounts.
concepts.analogy: One-sided: one shoe is missing. Two-sided: both shoes are on the wrong feet — still a pair, but wrong.
concepts.work: A trial balance difference tells you that at least one one-sided error exists. Its amount is a clue: a difference divisible by 9 often points to transposed digits (₹5,600 written as ₹6,500).

concepts.title: Rectifying before the trial balance
body: Two-sided errors: pass a journal entry that cancels the wrong part and records the right part. Method: write the correct entry, write the wrong entry that was made, and pass the entry that turns one into the other.
One-sided errors: no journal entry. Make a correcting posting in the affected account only, with an explanatory narration ("By Under-casting of Sales Book").
concepts.analogy: Correct entry − wrong entry = rectifying entry.
concepts.work: In software you cannot write "one-sided" corrections — every voucher must balance. That is why companies use a suspense or "errors" account and journal vouchers for every correction.

concepts.title: After the trial balance: the suspense account
body: If final accounts must be prepared before errors are found, the trial balance difference is placed in a Suspense Account.
When errors are found, one-sided errors are rectified through the Suspense Account (it takes the other side of the entry); two-sided errors are rectified as usual between the two accounts.
When all errors are found, the suspense account closes automatically. Wrong-side postings are corrected with double the amount.
concepts.analogy: The suspense account is a "lost and found" box — every one-sided error you fix takes its amount out of (or puts it into) the box until the box is empty.
concepts.work: Auditors ask for a list of all items cleared from suspense with the evidence for each — a balance written off without explanation is a red flag.

concepts.title: Next accounting period and the effect on profit
body: Once last year's books are closed, nominal accounts of that year no longer exist. Errors affecting last year's profit are corrected through a Profit & Loss Adjustment Account; its balance is then transferred to Capital (or partners' capital).
Errors affecting only real or personal accounts are corrected directly in those accounts.
Effect on profit: correcting an expense or loss upward, or an income downward, reduces profit; the opposite increases it. Corrections between personal or real accounts do not affect profit.
concepts.analogy: You cannot rewrite last year's report card, but you can add a note to this year's file saying last year's marks were understated.
concepts.work: Prior-period errors are reported carefully in financial statements; at Intermediate level you will meet the accounting standard that deals with them.

jobs.title: Clearing a suspense account before the audit
jobs.role: Accounts assistant at a CA firm (accounting outsourcing)
jobs.situation: A client's books show a suspense balance of ₹18,450 at the year end. The partner wants it cleared or explained before the books go to the auditor.
steps: Check the arithmetic of every subsidiary book total and carry-forward.
Compare the cash book with the bank statement for amounts posted differently.
Look for differences divisible by 9 (transposed digits) and by 2 (wrong-side postings).
For every error found, pass a rectifying entry through suspense and keep a working paper listing each one.
Explain any small residual balance to the partner rather than writing it off quietly.
jobs.takeaway: Rectification is detective work: the size of the difference often tells you where to look.
jobs.think: The difference is ₹1,800. Why might you look for a posting of ₹900 on the wrong side?
jobs.answer: A wrong-side posting moves the trial balance by double the amount: ₹900 on the wrong side creates a difference of ₹1,800.

jobs.title: An error of principle that changes profit
jobs.role: Junior auditor reviewing fixed asset additions
jobs.situation: While vouching additions to Building account you find invoices for painting and leak repairs totalling ₹2,40,000.
steps: Check whether the work improves the building (capital) or only maintains it (revenue).
Painting and leak repairs maintain the building — revenue expenditure.
Propose the rectification: Repairs A/c Dr, To Building A/c ₹2,40,000.
Note the effect: profit is overstated by ₹2,40,000 (and so is the building) until corrected.
jobs.takeaway: Errors of principle never show up in the trial balance — only judgement and documents reveal them.
jobs.think: Will this error affect the trial balance agreement?
jobs.answer: No. Both the debit and the credit were recorded equally; only the classification is wrong.

mcqs.q: Purchase of a computer for office use debited to Purchases account is an error of:
mcqs.explain: An error of principle arises when a transaction is recorded against a basic accounting principle, such as treating capital expenditure as revenue. A computer for office use is a fixed asset, but debiting Purchases treats it as goods for resale. The tempting option, error of commission, involves the right type of account but the wrong specific account or amount, such as posting to the wrong customer. In practice: auditors scan large purchase invoices to catch capital items wrongly booked as purchases.

mcqs.q: Which error affects the agreement of the trial balance?
options: Credit sale to Ravi posted to Rahul's account
A credit purchase not recorded at all
mcqs.explain: Under-casting the sales book understates only the Sales Account; customer accounts are posted correctly, so this one-sided error makes the trial balance disagree by ₹500. Posting to Rahul instead of Ravi, and debiting repairs to Machinery, put the correct amount on the correct side, while a completely omitted purchase affects neither side. The tempting option is repairs debited to Machinery — wrong account, but debits still equal credits. In practice: casting errors are found by re-totalling day books.

mcqs.q: Cash received from Anu ₹3,000 was posted to the debit of her account. The rectifying entry (after the trial balance) is:
mcqs.explain: Anu should have been credited with ₹3,000 but was debited with ₹3,000. To correct, her account must be credited ₹3,000 to cancel the wrong debit and a further ₹3,000 to give the right credit — ₹6,000 in all. Cash was correct, so the other side goes to Suspense: Suspense A/c Dr. To Anu ₹6,000. The tempting ₹3,000 only cancels the wrong debit. In practice: wrong-side postings always need double the amount to correct.

mcqs.q: A suspense account opened to agree the trial balance has a credit balance of ₹2,400. The trial balance had:
options: The debit side ₹2,400 more than the credit side
The credit side ₹2,400 more than the debit side
mcqs.explain: A suspense account is credited when the credit side of the trial balance is short. A credit balance of ₹2,400 therefore means the debit side was ₹2,400 more than the credit side, and the suspense credit made the totals agree. The tempting option, 'the credit side ₹2,400 more', would have needed a debit to suspense instead. In practice: accountants use the suspense balance's side to decide which side to search first for errors.

mcqs.q: Salary of ₹12,000 was posted to the Salary account as ₹1,200. Rectification will reduce profit by:
mcqs.explain: Salary Account was debited with ₹1,200 instead of ₹12,000, so expenses were understated by ₹12,000 − ₹1,200 = ₹10,800. Rectifying it debits Salary with a further ₹10,800, increasing expenses and reducing profit by ₹10,800. The tempting ₹12,000 treats the whole salary as omitted, ignoring the ₹1,200 already recorded. In practice: payroll reconciliations — comparing the salary register with the salary ledger — catch such posting errors before year end.

mcqs.q: Errors relating to last year's nominal accounts are corrected in the current year through:
options: Trading Account of the current year
Capital Account directly, item by item
mcqs.explain: Last year's nominal accounts have already been closed to profit and loss, so errors in them cannot be corrected through the current year's accounts directly. They are corrected through a Profit & Loss Adjustment Account (prior period items), whose net balance is transferred to Capital. The tempting option, the current year's Trading Account, would distort the current year's profit with last year's errors. In practice: companies disclose material prior period items separately so that current-year results are not misread.

mcqs.q: A trial balance difference of ₹2,700 is most likely caused by:
options: Transposing the digits of an amount (e.g. ₹4,100 as ₹1,400)
mcqs.explain: When two digits of an amount are reversed, the difference is always divisible by 9: ₹4,100 − ₹1,400 = ₹2,700, and 2,700 ÷ 9 = 300. So a difference divisible by 9 points to transposed digits. The other options — omitting a transaction, posting to the wrong customer, an error of principle — do not affect the trial balance at all. In practice: accountants hunting a difference first test whether it divides by 9 and then check amounts for swapped digits.

mcqs.q: Two errors — Wages account over-cast by ₹700 and Commission Received account over-cast by ₹700 — are:
options: Two-sided errors that need a suspense entry
mcqs.explain: Compensating errors are two or more errors that cancel each other's effect on the trial balance. Over-casting Wages (a debit) by ₹700 and Commission Received (a credit) by ₹700 adds ₹700 to both sides, so the trial balance still agrees. The tempting option, two-sided errors needing a suspense entry, is wrong because the trial balance agrees and no suspense account is opened. In practice: compensating errors are hard to detect and often surface only during detailed audit checks.

questions.q: Explain errors of omission, commission, principle and compensating errors with one example each.

items: Omission — a transaction left out wholly or partly. Example: a credit sale to Geeta not entered in the sales book.
Commission — wrong amount, account, side or total within the right class. Example: cash received from Tarun credited to Varun.
Principle — violation of an accounting principle, usually capital vs revenue. Example: purchase of a delivery van debited to Purchases.
Compensating — errors that cancel each other. Example: Rent account over-cast by ₹500 and Sales account over-cast by ₹500.

remarks: Examples should be specific (names and amounts) — generic examples earn less.
mistakes: Giving an error of commission as an example of principle.
tips: One line meaning + one line example for each.

summary: Errors arise in recording, posting, casting, balancing or copying to the trial balance.
One-sided errors disturb the trial balance; two-sided errors do not.
Before trial balance: journal for two-sided, ledger note for one-sided. After: one-sided go through suspense.
Next year: nominal items through Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c, balance to capital.
remember: Correct entry − wrong entry = rectifying entry.
Wrong-side posting is corrected with double the amount.
A difference divisible by 9 hints at transposed digits.
traps: Don't route two-sided errors through suspense.
Don't forget that personal-account corrections have no effect on profit.
Don't debit last year's nominal accounts in the new year — use P&L Adjustment.

viva.q: Name the four kinds of errors in accounting.

For example, a sale left out completely is an omission, posting to Sumit instead of Amit is commission, machinery debited to purchases is principle, and two errors of the same amount on opposite sides are compensating.

cases.title: Kabir & Co. — errors found after the trial balance
cases.case: The trial balance of Kabir & Co. on 31 March 2027 did not agree and the difference was put to a Suspense Account. Later these errors were found: (a) the Sales Book was overcast by ₹2,000; (b) furniture bought for ₹15,000 for office use was debited to Purchases Account; (c) cash of ₹3,000 received from Ravi was credited to his account as ₹300. After rectifying these errors the Suspense Account closed.

mcqs.q: What was the opening balance of the Suspense Account?
mcqs.explain: Error (a): the Sales Book overcast makes the credit side ₹2,000 too large. Error (c): Ravi was credited ₹300 instead of ₹3,000, making the credit side ₹2,700 too small. Net, the credit side was short by ₹2,700 − ₹2,000 = ₹700, so Suspense was credited with ₹700. Error (b) is two-sided. The tempting ₹700 Dr gets the side wrong. In practice: accountants work out each error's effect on each side before netting.

Furniture for office use is a capital asset, but debiting Purchases treats it as goods for resale (revenue). Treating capital expenditure as revenue breaks a basic accounting principle, so this is an error of principle. The tempting option, error of commission, involves posting to the wrong account of the same class, such as the wrong customer. In practice: such errors understate both fixed assets and profit, so auditors review large purchase entries for capital items.

mcqs.q: What is the rectifying entry for error (c)?
mcqs.explain: Ravi was credited with ₹300 instead of ₹3,000, so his account needs a further credit of ₹3,000 − ₹300 = ₹2,700. Cash was recorded correctly, so the other side of the rectifying entry goes to Suspense: Suspense A/c Dr. To Ravi ₹2,700. The tempting ₹3,000 credits the full amount again, ignoring the ₹300 already credited. In practice: customer statement disputes often reveal such short postings.

mcqs.q: What is the combined effect of the three rectifications on net profit (ignore depreciation)?
mcqs.explain: Rectifying (a) debits Sales ₹2,000, so profit falls by ₹2,000. Rectifying (b) moves ₹15,000 from Purchases to Furniture, reducing expenses, so profit rises by ₹15,000. Rectifying (c) affects only Ravi and Suspense, not profit. Net = ₹15,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹13,000 increase. The tempting ₹15,000 forgets the sales overcast. In practice: before finalising accounts, a CA prepares this profit impact summary for all rectifications found.
